newsitem.title: FRANCE: France shifts goalposts on EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: France shifts goalposts on EMU entry.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government has shifted the goalposts for entry to a single currency by admitting what everyone already suspected, that it will not cut its deficit this year to three percent of GDP.

But economists said the announcement may not make much difference to the EMU debate, with the real question still being whether Europe can revive economic growth enough to cut unemployment and sustain deficit reduction into next year.
"The goal has been shifted from three to three and a half," Adolf Rosenstock, economist at IBJ in Frankfurt said.
"People in the market will accept up to three and a half under the condition that 1998 will look better. If we can believe three percent next year, that would be accepted."
French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday the deficit would not be cut to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product as the previous centre-right government said.
"When you say you are not at three percent, that also means you are not at 3.1 percent either, but I cannot tell you how far we are beyond that," he told a business conference.
French daily Liberation said the government had an unofficial 1997 target of 3.3 percent after 4.2 percent in 1996.
The finance ministry declined comment, though this target would comply with the Maastricht treaty which requires deficits to show a trend towards three percent of GDP.
One European source said this month a deficit/GDP ratio of 3.3 percent or below would probably be accepted for single currency entry in 1999, while 3.4 percent or over would not.
Wim Duisenberg, president-elect of the European Monetary Institute, also repeated his opposition on Friday to an overly rigid interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.
"I want to keep away from this sort of fetishism about figures," he told Dutch daily Het Financieele Dagblad.
The key to France's new stance is the fact that its main ally Germany looks unlikely to meet the targets itself.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Friday it would be hard to meet the deficit target and almost impossible to cut its debt to the required 60 percent of GDP.

Rosenstock said he thought German people were tired of debate about the figures, particularly after Finance Minister Theo Waigel's ugly row with the Bundesbank over a plan to revalue its gold reserves to bolster public finances this year.

"I see more and more people getting less emotional about the whole thing but more and more cynical," he said. "My feeling is that people are feeling fed up. It's a fatalistic view. It (EMU) is going to come," he said.

Economists said an easing of Maastricht could make it easier for Italy, Spain and Portugal to join EMU at the start -- though in the classic bind of EMU logic they can only win provided Germany does not then insist on postponing the project.

"Spain could do without all of this. It appears to have everything going quite nicely. It would much rather see France and Germany hit their deficit targets," Darren Williams, economist at UBS in London, said.

The risk to the project is not so much what happens in 1997, but that either Germany fears deficits will overshoot in the years to come, undermining the euro, or France believes the single currency will make it impossible to cut unemployment.
Neither Paris or Bonn are yet backing away from the euro, but both are staking out the battleground for the months ahead.

"This is not a debate about decimal points, but rather a question of trust in a stable euro for the financial markets and public," Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a leading figure in the Christian Social Union (CSU) told Bild newspaper.
French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin meanwhile told ministers on Thursday that while France would respect its European commitments, it must give "absolute priority" to boosting jobs.

So far some believe the new government in France is falling into the same trap as previous prime minister Alain Juppe -- unable because of Maastricht constraints to take action to boost growth enough to bring down the deficit and unemployment.
Newspapers are already beginning to quip about a "Juppe-II" government after Jospin postponed plans to cut Value Added Tax (sales tax) to next year and insisted on capping spending.
"They are still stuck in that fiscal squeeze which has been very damaging for the last four years," Williams said.

"There is no growth initiative at all," Merrill Lynch economist Joanne Perez said. "They are finding the Maastricht constraints harder than they thought. We are seeing a relaxation of a lot of their commitments," she added.
